title: Newcastle’s stadium, finances and dismal form on the agenda as PIF delegation arrives for summit
content:
Yasir Al-Rumayyan will lead a 25-strong delegation of PIF officials flying in for Newcastle United’s board-level meetings in Northumberland this week.

The club’s chairman and governor of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), Newcastle’s 85 per cent owners, will hear from senior figures throughout the club, including Eddie Howe, the head coach, and David Hopkinson, the CEO, during an annual ‘off-siting’ conference at Matfen Hall, the luxury country hotel 16 miles west of Newcastle, on Wednesday and Thursday.

Hopkinson has confirmed that Newcastle’s plans for their stadium — with a decision to be made on whether to expand St James’ Park or build a new ground nearby — and their training ground, with a site identified at Woolsington near Newcastle International Airport, will be on the agenda, as will his already approved plan to turn the club into one of the world’s best by 2030.

Around 25 PIF officials, according to Hopkinson, will be joined by Jamie Reuben, the minority owner, and are also expected to seek answers for Newcastle’s underperformance on the pitch this season, with the club 14th in the Premier League after losing nine of their last 12 top-flight matches.

“We’re considering what to do with our stadium, whether that’s a significant renovation or a brand-new stadium,” Hopkinson told the SportsPro London conference at the Oval cricket ground, where he was speaking on Wednesday morning.

“We need more capacity to drive that revenue. Our training ground is very good — it’s not as good as others. If we’re going to have world-class ambition, we need world-class infrastructure to support that. These are the types of conversations we’re going to have over the next couple of days.”

The chief executive also touched upon Newcastle’s transfer policy moving forward, suggesting that the club will look to target younger players or less-expensive additions who they believe have a high ceiling for growth.

As The Athletic reported this week, Newcastle are exploring the possibility of selling Yoane Wissa this summer, likely for a significant loss, less than a year after signing him for £55million ($74.3m). Expensive acquisitions who do not work out, such as Wissa, are particularly damaging for a challenger club like Newcastle.

“We’ve got to be looking for those opportunities in the marketplace to join our squad where we think we can acquire them either early in their career or where we think there’s a value gap and use our money most effectively. And what we cannot do is overpay,” Hopkinson said.

The Canadian also trailed imminent new senior management announcements, saying the club had hired a new chief revenue officer (CRO) and a new chief marketing officer (CMO).

Hopkinson claimed Newcastle have recruited a “superstar” for the CMO role, while The Athletic has learned that Dave O’Connor will start as CRO in June. A Geordie who has built an agency in Switzerland, Newcastle view luring O’Connor home as a coup.

“We’ll be making these two announcements in the coming days,” Hopkinson said. “A superstar, an international. He’s going to focus on our digital growth. We cannot achieve all that ambition on Newcastle’s local market opportunity. We’ve got to go global.”

These new hires will be crucial in helping Hopkinson further pump-prime Newcastle’s revenue streams, as he looks to deliver his ambitious “Vision 2030” blueprint.

Although Newcastle’s figures will have grown again across the current season, 2024-25 is the most recent year when financial results are publicly available for Premier League clubs. Across that campaign, Newcastle’s turnover (£335.3m), matchday income (£51.6m) and commercial revenue (£120.2m) were dwarfed by the average of English football’s ‘Big Six’ clubs (at £638.8m, £119m and £288.2m respectively), so they have ground to make up.

Newcastle confirmed their first-ever training-ground sponsor earlier this month, with KNOX Hydration paying £6m-a-year for the rights. But Hopkinson believes that Newcastle can extract up to £100m more annually from commercial partnerships and untapped digital opportunities, citing car and insurance sponsors as two potential opportunities to explore.

“Our ambition is ultimately to be number one,” he said. “How are we going to do that? Frankly, money is the biggest piece of the equation. We’ve got to just generate more revenue, give ourselves a bigger envelope to work with. If we can execute superbly, there might be £100m in annual run rate revenue that could be unlocked.

“We’re (at) about £400m (for revenue, actually £335m for 2024-25 although that is expected to rise further for 2025-26). Well, that can become £500m, or stretch to £550m. We start to kick our way into that conversation. That’s our ambition.”

By Newcastle correspondent Chris Waugh

Howe was asked about Newcastle’s Matfen meetings after the Arsenal defeat and, though he said he expected them to be “slightly harder” for himself on a personal level given the downturn in the team’s form, Hopkinson is the first executive to offer an insight into what exactly can be expected to emerge from these ownership-level discussions.

Hopkinson hotfooted it straight from central London to Northumberland on Wednesday after taking part in this conference, so that he could be ready to welcome a 25-strong delegation from PIF and he will doubtless be asked for an update on how Newcastle are going to fulfil his sky-high aspirations by the end of the decade.

Hopkinson has been bold and ultra-ambitious in his public pronouncements since arriving at Newcastle in September, yet the chief executive knew that to carry any sort of momentum he had built with his vision forwards, actions needed to follow.

The groundbreaking training-ground sponsorship with KNOX was a start, but further bespoke and innovative commercial deals must quickly follow because, as he repeatedly stresses, on-field success strongly correlates with revenue and subsequent expenditure.

With Newcastle labouring on the field, it is vital that off-the-pitch progress continues. Further fortifying the executive-level structure feels important to that and, while Hopkinson adding senior staff has been trailed for months, actually having those new positions filled means those figures can get on with their jobs. If they are as well qualified as Hopkinson suggests, then their impact upon business operations should be consequential.

Hopkinson’s plan has already been signed off at boardroom level and he is in regular dialogue with the ownership, but the his first attendance at one of these annual ‘off-sitings’ offers a fresh opportunity for the CEO to get further input from those above him. Previous executives have found the pace of PIF decision-making painfully slow, but Hopkinson has to try and push the ownership to make critical infrastructure calls this week as a minimum.
